title: Formal Methods for Every Engineer in an AI-Powered Future

segments.text: The decisions you're making right now
about AI adoption, architecture
trade-offs, and how your team works
together will shape your systems for
years. Getting those calls right when
the landscape is shifting this fast is
hard.
QCon San Francisco has spent 20 years
connecting senior engineers with
practitioners who are a few steps ahead
on the same problems.
This November the 16th through 20th,
60-plus speakers across 12 tracks will
share what's actually working in
production and what isn't.
No hidden product pitches.
Just senior practitioners helping senior
practitioners.
Learn more at qconsf.com.
>> [music]
>> Hello there, folks. This is Shane Hastie
for the InfoQ Engineering Culture
Podcast. Today, I'm sitting down with
Gabriella Moreira.
Gabriella,
welcome. Thank you for taking the time
to talk to us.
>> Thank you. Thank you for having me.
>> My normal starting point in these
conversations is who's Gabriella?
>> I am a formal methods person. I think
that's the first thing I should say, and
I'm very passionate about this field,
and I've been working on trying to make
formal methods more accessible for like
about 8 years since I was starting to
have to decide what I was going to do
for my bachelor's thesis. I was
introduced to compilers, and I was very
passionate about compilers, specifically
like type systems. So, I did some
research work on type systems, some
stuff for Haskell. And then, when I was
trying to figure out what to do for my
bachelor's thesis, someone introduced
TLA+ to me, which is a formal
specification language. This is a person
that worked with me, and he was like, "I
saw this TLA+ thing, and I think you
will like it. You should take a look. I
still don't know why he thought that,
but I'm glad he did cuz I really, really
loved it. TLA+ is very like mathematical
specification language where you can
define what your system can do and the
properties. And I was really like in
love with it and I started doing tooling
for TLA+ for my bachelor thesis and then
I went into my master's, continued
developing tooling for TLA+ and doing
research there. And at the same time I
was working in the industry. I was
working with like event-driven
distributed systems and understanding
how difficult it is to handle all of the
corner cases, all of the scenarios, and
how it's expected that those developers
just come up with everything in our
heads. And I was like, "This TLA+ thing
should be used more. Like this is
perfect for what I'm doing." And at the
same time doing my master's and then I
was presenting at the TLA+ conference
and this company, Formal Systems, where
I work for, were there at the conference
as well and they found me. We were
basically doing the same kind of tooling
for TLA+ and naturally they wanted to
hire me and I joined Formal Systems then
4 years ago. I started building like
more tools for making Formal Methods
more accessible.
And the tool that I've been building for
the last 4 years is called Quint, which
is a new specification language based on
TLA+. The parts of TLA+ that were too
difficult for our new people to learn,
we tried to fix that and have Quint make
this more accessible version of TLA+
bringing all the good stuff while just
making it easy to use.
So yeah, that's my background and now
Formal Systems is making Quint a
spin-out. So we're spinning out Quint
and I'm CEO on this new initiative cuz
this Quint has been my baby since day
one. So naturally like I've transitioned
into this lead developer role into CEO
like over this last month.
>> So why should software engineers care
about formal methods?
>> I think we already care. We just I think
formal methods is more of like a
solution. I think people do think like,
"Oh, I should get into this formal
methods thing. I should learn." Like
they feel this responsibility,
but I don't really like that. I prefer
to see formal methods as a solution to a
problem they already have. A large part
of software engineering community has
this problem of like not being able to
think about all of the edge cases, all
of the corner cases of the complex
systems we are developing. Sure that
some systems are fairly trivial, but
most systems have this degree of
complexity where different sequences of
events can lead to different outcomes
and it's super hard to think about all
of the possible sequences. And the
sequences can be like the scheduler of
your operational system and when do you
get the lock?
Or it can be the sequences of what the
users intend to do in your interface,
right? Can be at very different levels.
So all of us are thinking about these
things all the time. And formal methods
really help us think about that. It It
helps us define what are the sequences,
what are the behaviors, and what are the
properties about those behaviors, and
then check things and actually find
corner cases, which might be problems or
not, but it helps us find those corner
cases and and understand better our the
systems we are building. So I think it's
more of a solution than like a
responsibility or something you have to
learn.
>> All right. So if I am a software
engineer facing one of these complex
environments where sequence of events is
likely to have an impact on me, what
should I do?
>> Well, right now, in 2026, you should try
to ask your favorite AI to write some
formal specification for you. Things are
much easier now than it was like a year
ago even, right? Where you had to like
learn a new language, learn how to use
these new tools, how to think in state
machines. Right now you can get a much
easier start. So like describing your
problem or solution, describing your
system to some AI and asking come and
write like a clean specification for me,
or even a TLA+ specification if you're
really into math,
and you want to see the math symbols.
Just getting the AI to write something
for you, and then not just like reading
the specification it produced, but
running it. Cuz running it is where you
get most value. So you go and like,
okay, now run it like model check it or
give me some behaviors. Cuz the
specification, the model is a state
machine in which I'm talking about the
kind of more formal methods I mean to.
So, you're going to define some state
machine and therefore you can see the
behaviors of that state machine. You
start in some initial state and you go
here, here, and there and you can see
how it behaves. And like, oh, now give
me a behavior that does this. Now give
me a behavior that reaches that. And you
can start understanding your system.
>> How is this different from just good
test design?
>> Test is hard and maybe it's getting a
bit easier now with some some tools, but
when you're talking just about
high-level user interactions with a
system and like maybe REST APIs,
that's fairly easy to test and then you
can get some like clean test that you
can read and look at. But in most cases
or complex cases where you actually get
most value out of this, it's hard to
write tests. It's hard to control when
your computer's scheduler is going to
decide when someone gets a lock or not.
It's hard to control time. It's hard to
control a bunch of things on like
message delays and and and all of that.
So, when you have a distributed system
or concurrent system, it's hard to write
tests for the things you're mostly
worried about. And when you're on a
formal methods specification, you are
actually on a more much more abstract
level where you can reason about these
things. The tools can also help come up
with the scenarios for you while most
tests you are the ones that have to like
define the scenarios, right? In formal
methods you can say like, give me one
scenario where I reach
that super rare thing. And then the tool
will come up with a scenario for you.
And then you can leverage that for
testing. But you should do. You should
not just leave the formal methods there
in a corner and then forget about it
when you're doing testing. The formal
methods should be part of your testing
and should be part of your even like
production monitoring and everything
else you do in your developer life
cycle.
>> So, how do we integrate this into our
workflows?
>> Again, in 2026 it's much easier and you
can get first like generate your first
back. Okay, now when you're happy with
your specification, you have seen the
behaviors, you are happy with the type
of properties you defined.
And you're kind of confident that it's a
faithful representation of whatever you
want, your solution or the system you
already have. Then you can integrate
that for testing. And this is called a
model-based testing. So you're taking
your model, your spec, and based on that
you're writing tests. And this requires
you to write some sort of code that
replays behaviors from your model
against your code, your actual
implementation. So this replay code, we
often call it a glue code or even
harness code. This is annoying to write.
It's a very boring code. Like everything
you change right on the model or any
implementation, you have to like go and
update that code and it's like it's
annoying to maintain and I think that's
the main reason why like model-based
testing hasn't become a thing so far.
But like with AI, it really becomes
something completely different because
then you can just delegate that part of
because it's a very trivial piece of
code also to write, so it's easy to
generate. We actually last like
December, we developed this open source
library called Quint Connect, which is
specific to Rust, but the community
already developed several different
ones. I think there's one for TypeScript
for sure, uh one for Zig, and I think
there's also one for for Go, but this
one I think it's not open source yet.
Anyway, we we we did one for Rust first
and then people can could base their
selves on that and write different ones.
And this library, it allows you to
define this glue code with a very nice
interface that also works as like
guardrails for AI in the sense of like
it's a very easy for AI to generate the
code there without having to like invent
anything. It just fills the interfaces
and it works. So this testing code
becomes much easier to generate and to
maintain across changes and therefore be
more integrated into the environment.
And we're now working more into how to
also leverage the model for run-time
monitoring. So for the data
from production, right? Cuz what you
test is not always the same thing that's
your users do. So, we believe that like
the input that comes from production
from runtime is super important. And
then there's this technique called trace
validation, which is also like something
that's hard to make feasible because it
have to orchestrate your code. There's a
bunch of challenges there, but we do
believe that like with AI that will
become easier and we are going to focus
on developing infrastructure for that.
So, it's also connected to your like
runtime monitoring. Your formal
specifications also connected to that.
>> You made the point when we were chatting
earlier
of precision in defining behavior
is crucial even more crucial today in
the in this realm of generative AI. How
do we get that right?
>> With a lot of understanding.
Unfortunately, I think people do
sometimes come to techniques like formal
methods in search of like an answer,
like an easy way out that this just
gives you like some checkmark and say
like, "Hey, yes, go. Your code is
correct. Just ship it." There is no such
thing. I don't believe in such thing. I
think you don't only can get closer to
the checkmark if you have lots of
understanding. So, when you understand
your system more and more, you are able
to then define things like properties of
your system and and really like see one
behavior and say like, "Oh, this is good
or this is not good." So, you have to
define this either like by defining your
state machine itself in the model or by
defining properties about your state
machine and then refine your state
machine. And you have those properties
that determine which behaviors are
important and which ones are correct.
Then that can be leveraged for testing
and for defining whether your behaviors
from production are correct or not, too.
Cuz even if you can observe the
behaviors, if you don't have anything to
tell if it's correct or not, then you're
not getting much usefulness out of it.
>> So, you're giving me
what sounds almost like an abstraction.
Is it just another layer of abstraction?
At a practical level as an engineer
who's thinking about getting into formal
methods who's
looking at okay, I need to build my
first state machine. I need to
understand this. I'm I'm now hitting a
complex problem. Where do I start? What
do I do?
>> So, you have to start defining what your
system is or what your solution is in
some formal language, right? If you're
going to use formal methods. And then in
order to understand things, you start
running or model checking your
specification, right? So, first of all,
if you just have your model, you can get
some random execution of your model.
That's the best thing you can get and
that can give you some insight, right?
You see some random behavior of your
model. Start in this initial state and
you go here, go there.
And then you are going to look at that
and say, "Mhm, I don't like this. I
actually don't think I can go from this
state to that state. This sounds wrong."
So, you go and like write or refine your
model or you refine some property you
say, "I don't want this to happen." And
then you run again and then you run with
your property and verify your property.
And then there are some
different techniques we can use to get
more insight. For instance, when you're
thinking about distributed systems, we
often define failure modes,
which is not common like when you're
just writing the code or just writing
some pseudo code, you're not going to
define the failures, right? The failures
are something that happens in the
external world and and you are going to
handle those failures. But if failures
are important to you, if the point of
your software is to recover from
failures or act in such and such a way
upon failures, then you have to define
what those failures are and what's your
response to those failures. And this
helps you understand better how your
system behaves and what are the failures
and what are the properties of your
system upon failures.
So, if you have more failures than you
tolerate, what happens? Which ways your
software break? Because if you have more
failures than you tolerate, then you do
expect your software to break, right?
So, you go and you define that and then
you ask the again the model checker to
run or the some simulator to run, and it
will give you some behavior like, "Oh,
so that's how my system breaks. Okay,
now I understand. This makes sense. This
is according to my expectation." Or no,
this is different from my expectation.
You can also define what we call
witnesses, and these are properties that
you expect to break in order to witness
some behaviors, to see something
interesting happen. So, if you want to
challenge the tools and see how useful
the tools are for you, you can say like,
"What is the rarest, most difficult
thing that I can come up with? The most
edgy edge case, the most coronary case
that I I am a smart person. I developed
the system. What can I come up with?"
And you come up with this super rare
scenario, and you see if the tools can
find it.
And that gives you like some level of
confidence. If the tools are finding the
the scenario that you find is super
rare, then it means that probably the
tools are is at least as good as finding
corner cases as you are.
So, this is one technique you can do.
You can also use like these witnesses in
combination with properties in ways to
check that your properties are not being
checked in a vacuum.
And you can also define specific
behaviors that matter to you the most.
When you're defining a solution to a
problem, you usually have behaviors in
mind, like some specific behaviors,
right? So, like, "What if process B
tries to access this while process A
holds the lock?" You're thinking about
the sequences in your mind. So, when you
write those down in a reproducible way,
they become really valuable
documentation that you can like send to
your colleagues and communicate, and
they can run the same scenarios. So,
those things that we usually draw in
whiteboards, they can become something
executable without sacrificing
abstraction. Cuz when you're in a formal
language, you're saying the same
abstraction level as your whiteboards
are the very close level of abstraction
to whiteboards. Differently than
testing, where you have to like set up
all of these mock things and addresses
and data. So, this is also like one way
of making those abstractions something
concrete that you can look at, that you
can execute, that you can put in your PR
description, that's checked on CI, and
becomes like documentation in your
software. So, I'm really excited about
that part about the reproducible
behaviors.
Let me tell you about my experience in
formal systems. In formal systems has a
bunch of like PhDs and people that are
really smart in like distributed
systems. And I was working with
distributed systems, I
struggled to understand the most basic
protocols in the past. So I did struggle
with that. And everyone in formal
systems was like, "Oh, of course,
business in fault tolerance. Yes,
consensus." And they would talk about
these things so naturally and I was
behind.
And at some point like I
sat down and I wrote a formal
specification for one of the algorithms.
When I was writing the formal spec, I
still didn't understand. Just by writing
it was not sufficient, nearly sufficient
for me to understand the algorithm. But
then when I started running it, then I
started like having those witness for
those corner cases and then I understood
what the steps that led to the corner
cases were. When I finally managed to
write like one reproducible example for
the most corner case of the entire
algorithm, that's when I felt like I
understood it. And I still feel like I
did understood that algorithm. So it
felt really amazing for myself and
that's why I'm so excited to talk about
it and I want everyone to try it out. So
I really think that helps with
understanding and confidence.
>> What's the relationship between the
model and my code base?
>> That's a very good question. So the
relationship is usually like the model
should be more abstract than your code,
otherwise like you lose this power of
abstraction and you're basically just
reasoning about the code itself.
Although in some cases it still makes
sense because the code is harder to test
than this like cuz you're at least
abstracting away the hardware and stuff.
But how do you keep them in sync?
There are basically two techniques, the
model based testing technique that I
talked about already, like you replay
traces from your model against the code
and check that the resulting state in
your code matches the resulting state
from your model step by step. And you
can do model based testing with like
random behaviors or you can tune it to
like do remember that witness that I
wrote that was super rare scenario? Let
me test that. And remember that a
reproducible example that I wrote? Let's
test that. So that's model based testing
and the other technique is trace
validation, which is you somehow log,
register your production executions.
There's instrumentation things, or you
can just log, but you have to log some
information, and then based on that
information, that behavior from
production, you're going to try and ask
the model, like, is this compliant with
what you said?
And it's really important that you keep
them in sync. And historically,
people sometimes write models and then
leave them in like specs folder and
GitHub, and it could just go there to
die, and no one looks at it again.
And that is a problem, because I've
heard people, and it's I think it's very
painful to hear those stories, but it's
I've heard people that had a spec that
was correct, and the design was correct,
and the initial version of the code was
also correct, but over time, the code
deviated from the spec, and they had a
bug in production that was not present
in the model. I think that's a very sad
outcome for the person who put effort
into writing a specification, even
before AI and everything. There's
actually a case from AWS where this
happens in October last year. In that
case, the specification that they had
was not a formal one. It was just like
some documentation, and they've had this
DNS outage in October. It was actually
not a design flaw. The original code was
correct, and there was this bug that
happened was not a bug in the design,
and just the code diverged off from the
design over time, and they found a bug.
So, what they did, and this was
presented at a re:Invent conference from
AWS, what they did was make that model
formal, and then they used their AI tool
to compare like the new version of the
model with the code, and they actually
found the divergence just by AI looking
at the code and reading the code and
reading the model. If it found a
divergence, then they fixed the code,
and they said, "Okay, now they're not
divergent anymore." So, they learned a
lesson of like
when things don't stay in sync, then you
might deviate from your very careful and
well-thought-out original design, and
that's very sad.
>> But, that's been the case in software
engineering from time immemorial. I
recall as a COBOL programmer the problem
with keeping the design and the code in
sync.
>> Yeah, definitely it's not a new problem.
I think it's more like a new solution.
Not that formal methods are new. I think
these techniques like model-based
testing, trace validation, they are not
new. I cannot tell you how old they are,
but they they are at least 10 years old.
Because when I was
in my doing my bachelor's, I I was
already looking at this. So, they are at
least 10 years old, probably much older.
The thing is the solution that comes
with AI is a much better solution than
the solution without AI. Because now you
almost like don't have an excuse.
Because you can just so easily connect
that spec with the code now by having AI
generate this like glue code or this
instrumentation.
Or even like if you have logs, how do
you parse those logs to get extract the
behavior and check it against the spec?
All of these things are things that AI
is great at. Like with LM code
generation, if you use LMs to parse
logs, it's it's so good at that. Uh
and it's so boring to do that ourselves.
>> So, a new solution to an age-old problem
and then layering formal methods
in there.
What's the important question I haven't
asked you?
>> I think what does this mean for our
profession?
Yeah, so I think there is some
discussion going on online and some
overall concern about what do we do now?
What's what's left for our profession if
AI is is writing the code? And of
course, no one of us know how much AI is
going to write code, like what level of
code it can take away from us.
But, regardless, I think this
part of the profession of like thinking
about edge cases and defining what
behaviors are correct or not, it has to
be ours to take. Like it's not AI is not
taking that away from us. And when we
are able to define what we want and what
behaviors we want to see and what
behaviors we do not want to see in our
code. And that's not like for everyone.
I think in some cases like product
people that are not non-technical, they
will be able to leverage AI and this
this is already happening, right?
They're leveraging AI to generate some
sort of products. And then like safety
and then when there are no like big
concerns that works super well and I'm
glad it does. But still there's a lot of
software where the behaviors we have to
worry about are super complex and those
product people that don't have a
technical background, they will struggle
or they would have to learn this
technical part in order to do that. But
we know about concurrency issues, we
know about how difficult these things
are and thinking about all the possible
orderings of events. So, if we are able
to define that well, it can both help us
understand better and have a continued
understanding even if AI is writing the
code, we still understand what the
system is doing because we are
interacting with the system. And it can
also help us assert that the AI
generated code is correct
via these techniques that I've been
telling you about.
>> So, confidence in the product and value
in the profession.
>> Yes, and they're not taking away the fun
part from us. AI is not taking that
away.
>> Gabriela, a lot of interesting stuff
there. If people want to dive deeper, if
they want to continue the conversation,
where can they find you?
>> I'm on LinkedIn. I'm very active there.
So, if you want to follow me there or
connect,
LinkedIn is the way.
>> I will make sure those links are in the
show notes.
Gabriela, thank you so much for taking
the time to talk to us today.
>> [music]
>> Thank you. Thank you for having me and
for the great questions.
>> [music]
[music]
>> Mhm.
